newsitem.title: UK: Ex-wise man calls for post-election UK rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Ex-wise man calls for post-election UK rate rise.

text.p: The next British government will have to raise interest rates to cool a surging domestic economy and, unless tight public spending plans are enforced, taxes will have to rise too, a leading economist said on Friday.

Andrew Sentance, director of the London Business School's Centre for Economic Forecasting, said the real inflationary threat in Britain would be delayed until 1998, or as long as the pound's strength continued to hold down import prices.
"But after the election, a policy tightening will be needed to slow the economy and head-off the risk of a boom-bust cycle."
He said base rates, now at six percent, should have reached seven by early 1998, with a 0.5 percent increase needed soon after next Thursday's election.

Sentance, who previously served as one of Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's independent advisers or "wise men", said tight spending targets would also have to be maintained to avoid tax increases.
Clarke pencilled in rigorous limits in last November's budget and his opposite number, Labour's Gordon Brown, has promised to match them for the next two years.
Sentance said the targets were very tight but achievable. "But some selective tax increases...could be seen as an insurance policy against spending overruns," he said.
A tax rise would also have the advantage of taking the pressure off interest rates. Higher interest rates could force the pound up further.

Britain's exporters are already squealing about the pound's strength, which has made their goods more expensive abroad. Sterling has surged about 17 percent against other major currencies since last August.
A pre-emptive tax rise may also allow politically beneficial tax cuts later in the next parliament, Sentance said.

With the Labour party well ahead of the Conservatives in most opinion polls, it is Brown who is likely to face these dilemmas. But he has ruled out changing income tax rates or extending value-added tax to many areas.
On the positive side, Sentance forecast that economic growth would exceed three percent this year, with consumer spending rising four percent. Both will slow in 1998.
Underlying inflation would fall to 2.2 percent by the end of the year from 2.7 now. And best of all in electoral terms, unemployment would fall to less than 1.5 million, from about 1.7 million now.
Sentance urged the new administration not be lulled into a false sense of security by the seemingly golden scenario of steady growth and low inflation.

"The recent rise in pay increases and tightening in the labour market indicates an inflationary threat in 1998 and beyond," he said. The pound would inevitably drop back at some point, ending the downward pressure on import prices.
Average earnings are now rising five percent per annum, well above the prevailing inflation rate.
The pound's volatility makes the other great question facing the next British government -- whether to sign up for a single European currency -- fraught with danger.
Sentance said early entry would be foolish. "It would be reckless to take such a step without a much better track record of stability against other European currencies."

The pound crashed out of the European exchange rate mechanism in September 1992 and plunged below 2.20 marks until recovering last year. It has now pulled all the way back above its old ERM floor of 2.778 marks.
Sentance said a prolonged transition to EMU -- scheduled to start in January 1999 -- was a far safer bet for Britain.
Turning to Labour's plans to introduce a minimum wage, he warned that if set too too high, it could cost jobs. "The minimum wage should be set no higher than 3.50 pounds," Sentance said.
